summary: A proposal to add two File Transfer Protocol commands, ReaDMailFile and ReaDMail, that would let a user read mail stored at a site without logging in. They mirror the existing MLFL and MAIL commands for sending. The authors note that handling users with several IDs is left for later.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 458 proposes two FTP commands for reading mail from a network site without the usual login step. One sends mail on a separate data connection; the other sends it with FTP's replies.

questions: how to read mail via ftp
what are rdmf and rdml commands
subtitle: Two proposed FTP commands for reading mail stored at another site.

tldr.problem: Users could have mail at more than one network site, but reading it required logging in and using different retrieval methods.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 458 proposes RDMF and RDML as read counterparts to FTP's MLFL and MAIL commands. RDMF sends mail over the data connection; RDML sends mail and replies over the TELNET connection.
tldr.outcome: The proposal describes two ways to retrieve mail and leaves the problems of users with multiple IDs for later work.

today: The unit records RFC 458's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. The document is a proposal for FTP mail-retrieval commands.

sections.title: Why Add Mail-Reading Commands
sections.content:
FTP already had the MLFL and MAIL commands for sending mail. RFC 458 proposes matching commands for reading it, so a user could retrieve mail from one or more sites without logging in at each site or using different retrieval methods.

The authors say FTP's existing password protection could be used when security is required. They also identify the problem of different people sharing an ID, and one person having several IDs, but leave those issues unresolved.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal adds ways to read mail through FTP, matching its existing ways to send mail. It does not solve how to identify people who share or have several user IDs.

sections.title: Two Ways to Return Mail
sections.content:
RDMF (ReaDMailFile) transfers the mail over FTP's data connection. FTP replies use the TELNET connection. Its listed successful replies include 200, 250 and 330; the 200 reply carries the text NO MAIL NOW.

RDML (ReaDMail) sends both the mail and FTP replies over the TELNET connection. It introduces reply 152, meaning that mail text follows; that text may say NO MAIL NOW. The RFC also lists success and failure reply codes for both commands.
sections.plainLanguage: RDMF puts the mail on a separate data connection. RDML puts the mail and its status replies together on the TELNET connection.

sections.title: A Proposal for Network Mail
sections.content:
The authors suggest that a useful network mail system should let each person's mail reach one repository, ideally at a site the person chooses. They expect the proposed commands could be useful both in that arrangement and in the network as it then existed.

The RFC describes the commands as a proposal and does not report implementation or adoption. Its focus is mail retrieval; the identity problems it raises are explicitly left for other work.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors want mail to be gathered in one chosen place for each person. This RFC proposes retrieval commands but does not say that they were implemented.
